sources.author: Swyx (Shawn Wang)
sources.headline: Founder @ Latent Space | AI Engineer Podcast | ex-Netlify, AWS
sources.post_summary: Claude's new multi-agent orchestration patterns are changing how teams think about agentic workflows. Sharing our internal architecture for chaining 5+ specialized subagents without context bleed — the key insight is treating each agent like a stateless function with a strict input/output contract. Most teams getting this wrong are passing too much context upstream.

sources.author: Lior Ben David
sources.headline: AI Infrastructure Engineer @ Anthropic | prev Google DeepMind | Building at the frontier
sources.post_summary: We just open-sourced our internal agent evaluation harness. After 6 months of running production AI agents, we found MMLU and HumanEval completely useless for predicting real-world reliability. What actually matters: tool call accuracy under adversarial inputs, graceful degradation on ambiguous prompts, and cost-per-resolved-task. Link in comments.

sources.author: Cassidy Williams
sources.headline: CTO @ Contenda | Developer Experience Advocate | Speaker | ex-GitHub, Netlify
sources.post_summary: Hot take: the developer tool landscape in 2026 is bifurcating hard. One camp is building AI-native tools that assume your agent writes the code. The other is still bolting Copilot onto legacy IDEs. The gap between these two camps is going to be wider than the gap between mobile-first and desktop-first was in 2012. If your DevEx stack isn't agent-native, you're already behind.

sources.author: Alessio Fanelli
sources.headline: Managing Partner @ Decibel | prev CTO @ Memfault | Investing in infra + AI
sources.post_summary: We're seeing a Cambrian explosion in AI agent infrastructure — vector DBs, memory layers, orchestration frameworks, observability tools. But 80% of production outages we see in portfolio companies trace back to the same two problems: uncontrolled token spend and non-deterministic tool routing. The infra category is real but the winners will be whoever solves cost predictability first, not whoever has the best benchmark.

sources.author: Kyle Coleman
sources.headline: CMO at Clari | Pipeline Generation | GTM Strategy
sources.post_summary: Most outbound teams are measuring the wrong thing. They track activity (emails sent, dials made) but ignore signal quality. A rep who sends 20 highly-personalized emails to ICP accounts will outperform one sending 200 generic blasts every time. We rebuilt our entire SDR comp plan around signal-triggered outreach and pipeline velocity — not volume. Here's exactly how we did it.

sources.author: Saad Khan
sources.headline: GTM Engineer | Helping B2B teams build AI-native outbound systems | Ex-Salesforce
sources.post_summary: GTM engineering is not a job title. It's a forcing function. When one person can run a Clay table that does what 3 SDRs used to do — enrich, score, personalize, and sequence — the economics of outbound change permanently. I've now built 14 of these systems for Series A-C companies. The pattern is always the same: signal in, sequence out, human only for closing. Here's the exact stack.

sources.author: Melissa Rosenthal
sources.headline: Chief Creative Officer | B2B Content that doesn't suck | Advisor to 12 startups
sources.post_summary: Hot take: your content strategy is failing because your marketing team is writing for the algorithm instead of the buyer. I reviewed 60 LinkedIn company pages last week. Every single one led with features, not problems. Buyers don't care what your product does. They care about what breaks when they don't have it. Content that converts starts with the pain, not the pitch — and most teams have this completely backwards.

sources.author: Jacki Leahy
sources.headline: RevOps Therapist | Salesforce Architect | Turning CRM chaos into pipeline clarity
sources.post_summary: Every RevOps leader I talk to has the same problem: their CRM is a graveyard of bad data, and leadership still trusts the forecast. The fix isn't a new tool — it's a data contract between Sales, Marketing, and CS that gets enforced at the process level before anything hits Salesforce. I built a simple 3-field hygiene protocol that reduced forecast variance by 34% in one quarter. Sharing the template below.

sources.author: Priya Nair
sources.headline: Shipped 3 products in 12 months | Solo founder | ex-Google PM
sources.post_summary: Priya shares that she just hit $10k MRR with her second product — a Notion-to-landing-page tool built in a weekend. She breaks down the exact Cursor + Claude workflow she used to go from idea to deployed in 48 hours, and why she stopped waiting for a cofounder.

sources.author: Marcus Webb
sources.headline: Laid off → launched | 6 months into my first SaaS | sharing everything
sources.post_summary: Marcus documents his 6-month mark since getting laid off from a mid-size fintech. He's not profitable yet but has 47 paying users and just quit applying to jobs. The post is a raw honest comparison of his bank account then vs now, and why the fear was worse than the reality.

sources.author: Soo-Jin Park
sources.headline: Teacher → developer → founder | I build tools for burnt-out educators
sources.post_summary: Soo-Jin posts a screenshot of her first Stripe payment — $29 from a stranger. She was a middle school math teacher 18 months ago, taught herself to code at night, and just launched a lesson-planning AI tool for teachers. The post ends with 'I made this. From nothing. You can too.'

sources.author: Andrei Popescu
sources.headline: Solo dev shipping fast | Claude Code + Cursor daily driver | GTM engineer
sources.post_summary: Andrei posts a 7-day build log showing how he used Claude Code to build, test, and deploy a cold outreach personalization tool with zero outside help. He breaks down token costs vs. freelancer costs and argues that the real leverage shift in 2026 is context engineering, not just prompting.
